1. Recap: The Command
terraform workspace select was already introduced as a CLI command in the CLI module, this topic covers exactly what actually happens when you run it.
Switching is genuinely the most frequent, everyday workspace operation, far more common in practice than creating a new one.
Understanding it well, alongside the real risk covered later in this topic, is essential for anyone working across more than one real workspace regularly.
This topic also covers terraform.workspace, the reference that lets configuration itself respond to whichever workspace is currently active.

2. Switching Which State Is Active
Selecting a workspace genuinely determines which separate state every subsequent plan or apply actually operates against, until switched again.
Nothing about the configuration files themselves changes, exactly the same distinction already covered in the What are Workspaces topic.
This switch persists across separate terminal sessions, it is recorded in a local file, not something that resets automatically between commands.
Because of this persistence, it is genuinely easy to forget which workspace is currently active, covered directly as a real risk later in this topic.

3. terraform.workspace
Inside the configuration itself, the built-in reference terraform.workspace reads the name of whichever workspace is currently active, genuinely useful for conditional logic.
This reference requires no declaration at all, it is simply available, automatically, inside any expression anywhere in the configuration.
Recall conditional expressions from the Expressions & Functions module, terraform.workspace is very often paired directly with a ternary expression.
This is the one real, concrete way a configuration can genuinely behave differently per workspace, without needing separate variable files at all.

blocks.content: 4. A Real Use Case
Sizing an instance differently based directly on terraform.workspace, exactly the example above, is a genuinely common, real use of this reference.
Another genuinely real, common use scopes a resource's name using terraform.workspace, avoiding naming collisions between workspaces sharing a real, underlying provider.
This is often necessary specifically because, as covered honestly in the next topic, workspaces share the same real backend and credentials by default.
Naming resources this way keeps a workspace-per-environment setup genuinely usable in practice, not just in theory.

blocks.content: 5. A Real Risk
This is worth being direct about, forgetting which workspace is currently active before running apply is a genuine, real risk, always worth confirming with terraform workspace show first.
An apply run against the wrong workspace by mistake genuinely still succeeds, Terraform has no way to know that was not actually intended.
This real risk is precisely why the honest limits covered in the next topic matter, a mistaken apply here can genuinely affect real, live infrastructure.
Building a real, habitual check into every session's start is a small, genuinely worthwhile discipline.

blocks.content: 6. Confirming the Active Workspace
terraform workspace show prints exactly the currently active workspace, a fast, genuinely reliable way to confirm before running anything real.
This is the single most useful command from this entire topic to build into a real, habitual, pre-apply routine.
Unlike workspace list, which shows every workspace, show prints only the one that is currently, actually active, a faster, more direct check.
Making this check automatic, rather than remembered manually, is covered directly in the next section.

7. A Real, Visual Safety Net
Many real teams configure their shell prompt to directly display the active Terraform workspace, a genuinely visual, always-present safety net.
This removes the need to remember to run a separate check manually, the information is simply, visibly always there.
Several popular shell prompt frameworks support this directly, worth setting up once, deliberately, for anyone working across multiple real workspaces regularly.
This is a small, practical setup investment that genuinely pays for itself the first time it prevents a real, costly mistake.

blocks.content: 8. workspace new vs workspace select
Recall from the previous topic, new creates a brand new, empty workspace, select switches to one that already, genuinely exists.
Confusing the two is a genuinely easy mistake, attempting select on a workspace that does not exist yet fails clearly, rather than creating it silently.
This distinct, separate behavior is a deliberate, real safety choice, avoiding an accidental, unintended new workspace from a simple typo.
Keeping this distinction clear avoids a real, if minor, moment of confusion during everyday, real usage.

Building it into a real, shared runbook or CI pipeline step makes it consistent across an entire real team, not dependent on individual memory.

blocks.content: 11. Scripting Around the Active Workspace
CI/CD pipelines, covered in their own module ahead, often need to select the correct workspace automatically, rather than relying on a person remembering to do it.
A pipeline step can select, or create if missing, the correct workspace based on the branch or environment being deployed, removing the manual risk covered earlier entirely.
This kind of automation is genuinely one of the strongest real arguments for workspaces in a well-built, real CI/CD setup.
Building this pattern early, rather than relying purely on manual discipline, is worth the small, real upfront investment.
terraform workspace select "$ENVIRONMENT" || terraform workspace new "$ENVIRONMENT"

blocks.content: 12. What Switching Does Not Do
Switching workspaces genuinely does not run plan or apply automatically, it purely changes which state the next command targets, nothing executes on its own.
It also genuinely does not change any variable values automatically, unless the configuration itself is written to react to terraform.workspace, exactly as covered earlier.
Being clear about what switching does not do avoids a real, easy assumption that more happens automatically than actually does.
This honest, precise understanding is exactly what keeps the real risk from earlier in this topic from turning into an actual, costly mistake.
